SHANGHAI EVENING POST & MERCURY.
JAN 8 1940

Japanese Delay
Reuter Cables

Reports On Destruction
Of English Hospital
Said Held Up

Reuter telegrams from Tsingtao,
reporting the burning by Japan-
ese troops of the English Methodist
Mission hospital at Chuchia, near
Wutingfu, in Shantung, on Christ-
mas Day, were subjected to con-
siderable delays, it was stated here
today. The delays were presum-
ably caused by the Japanese cen-
sors.

The first message, filed from
Tsingtao on January 4 at 6.15 p.m.,
took over 48 hours in transmis-
sion, only reaching Shanghai after
7 p.m. on January 6.

A second message, in which the
Japanese authorities are reported
to have admitted the burning of
the hospital, was equally delayed.
It was filed from Tsingtao on
January 5 at 6 p.m., and did not
get to Shanghai until 2.15 p.m.
January 6.

"Normal" transmission time for
messages from Tsingtao to Shang-
hai by the Japanese-controlled
radio company, the only means of
communication, is about three
hours. According to the Shanghai
office of this company, conditions
during the past few days have
been "normal."

《上海晚邮报与信使报》
1940年1月8日

路透社电报遭日本方面延误

关于英国医院被毁的报道据称被扣留

据今日在此间称，从青岛发出的、报道日军于圣诞节当天在山东武定府附近朱家（Chuchia）焚烧英国卫理公会传教医院的路透社电报，遭受了严重延误。延误据推测是由日本检查员造成的。

第一份电报于1月4日下午6点15分从青岛发出，传输耗时超过48小时，直到1月6日晚上7点后才抵达上海。

第二份电报同样遭到延误，据报道日本当局在该电报中承认了焚烧医院一事。该电报于1月5日下午6点从青岛发出，直到1月6日下午2点15分才到达上海。

根据这家受日本控制的无线电公司（唯一的通信手段）上海办事处的说法，过去几天的状况属于“正常”，而从青岛到上海的讯息“正常”传输时间约为三小时。

CONFIDENTIAL
REPORT
SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE
S. B. REGISTRY
No. S. B. D. 2398
3.1, Special Branch Section
Date April 24, 1939

Subject Japanese Censorship - Cable companies and news report services.

Made by. D.S. Lockwood Forwarded by. C. Crawford. O.I.

Prior to the outbreak of the Sino-Japanese
hostilities in 1937 all Cable Companies and News
Services were supervised by a body appointed by the
Chinese National Government to censor out-going and
in-coming messages, whether commercial, private or
news reports. At the end of 1937 this body ceased
to operate following the retreat of the Chinese forces
from the environs of Shanghai. Subsequently the
Japanese authorities announced that they had assumed,
by right of conquest all the privileges of the
Chinese Government, and on January 6, 1938 Japanese
censors were appointed to the cable companies to
supervise all messages. The cable companies referred
the appointment of censors by the Japanese to their
respective Consulate-Generals, when the action of
the Japanese was approved.

The Japanese censors work on similar lines
to their Chinese predecessors. With regard to
commercial messages, whether in code or plain language,
a certificate is required from the Consular represent-
ative certifying that no illegal business is being
transacted. Private and personal cablegrams are not
interfered with but, they are all scrutinised by the
censors. News reports are however, supervised when
items and words derogatory to the Japanese are deleted.
If it is considered necessary to censor items of news
the decision is conveyed to the news correspondent
with the request that it be amended or he is informed

主题 日本审查制度 - 电报公司与新闻通讯社。

撰写人：D.S. Lockwood 转呈人：C. Crawford. O.I.

在1937年中日敌对行动爆发之前，所有电报公司和新闻通讯社均由中国国民政府任命的一个机构进行监管，该机构负责审查 outgoing（发出）和 incoming（接收）的电文，无论是商业、私人还是新闻报道。1937年底，随着中国军队从上海周边撤退，该机构停止运作。随后，日本当局宣布，凭借征服者的权利，他们已接管中国政府的所有特权，并于1938年1月6日向各电报公司派驻日本检查员，以监督所有电文。各电报公司将日本方面任命检查员一事提请各自总领事馆裁决，日本方面的行动由此获得批准。

日本检查员的工作方式与其中国前任类似。关于商业电文，无论是密码还是明文，均需领事代表出具证明，证实其中不涉及非法交易。私人和个人电报不受干涉，但均经检查员 scrutinised（仔细审查）。然而，新闻报道受到监管，其中贬低日本的内容和词汇会被删除。如果认为有必要审查某些新闻项目，决定会传达给新闻通讯员，要求其修改，或者被告知

    It is the concensus of opinion among the
managers of local cable companies that during the past
four months the censors have been very lenient as regards
news reports transmitted abroad. The reason for this
is attributed to other facilities available to newspaper
correspondents who wish to transmit confidential
messages to their agencies; the broadcasting of news
bulletins and the utilisation of the systems of the
Globe Wireless Company of 51, Canton Road and Press
Wireless Inc., of 1-3, Kiukiang Road (American)
and other concerns.

    The impression gained is that the Japanese
censors confine themselves to prevent anti-Japanese
messages or words harmful to Japanese prestige from
being incorporated in messages or comments on the
Sino-Japanese situation. This factor coupled with
the fact that previous attempts to suppress news have
failed, can be described as the main reason for the
present moderate attitude of the Japanese censors in
Shanghai.

    当地电报公司经理们的普遍意见是，在过去四个月里，检查员对于发往国外的新闻报道非常宽大。其原因归因于那些希望向其机构发送机密消息的报纸记者拥有其他便利渠道；即通过广东路51号环球无线电公司（Globe Wireless Company）和九江路1-3号美商Press Wireless Inc.（新闻无线公司）以及其他公司的系统广播新闻简报。

    给人的印象是，日本检查员仅限于防止反日信息或有损日本威望的词汇被纳入电文或关于中日局势的评论中。这一因素，加上此前压制新闻的尝试均告失败的事实，可以说是目前上海日本检查员采取温和态度的主要原因。

December 26, 1938. Morning Translation

Standard and other local newspapers :-

JAPANESE AUTHORITIES AND THE LOCAL TELEGRAPH COMPANIES

The Great Northern Telegraph Company (a Danish concern), the Great Eastern Telegraph Company (a British concern) and the Pacific Telegraph Company (an American concern) on Avenue Edward VII had formerly concluded an agreement with the Ministry of Communications of the National Government whereby the right of despatching telegrams would be restored to China and a portion of the earnings of the three companies would be paid to the Ministry of Communications. After the withdrawal of the Chinese forces from Shanghai, the Japanese detailed officials to the three companies to censor telegrams.

It is now learned that the three telegraph companies have received a notification from the Japanese demanding that the portion of their earnings which used to be handed over to the Ministry of Communications of the National Government be deposited in the Yokohama Specie Bank. The three companies are understood to be considering ways and means to deal with the request.

CHINA PRESS.

SEP 28 1938

Japanese Censors
Suppress Telegram
On Mission Bombing

A further example of the Japanese censors' activities in suppressing incoming Reuter telegrams was revealed yesterday when Reuters Shanghai Office received from Hongkong copies of recent telegrams dispatched by Reuters Hongkong office to Shanghai.

One telegram related details of the bombing of the Stout Memorial Hospital of the South China Mission at Wuchow. This was dispatched from Hongkong at midnight on September 18-19 but has not yet been delivered to Reuters Shanghai office.

The telegram in question, as sent off by Reuters Hongkong office, ran:

"Canton. Reliably learned Stout Memorial Hospital of South China Baptist Mission at Wuchow bombed on September 17 by nine Japanese planes which scored five direct hits on buildings. None of American members staff injured but damage estimated $150,000."

《字林西报》

1938年9月28日

日本检查员
压制关于传教士医院
被轰炸的电报

昨天揭露了日本检查员压制 incoming（接收）路透社电报活动的又一例证，当时路透社上海办事处收到了来自香港的、由路透社香港办事处发给上海的近期电报副本。

其中一份电报详细描述了华南传教团位于梧州（Wuchow）的斯托特纪念医院（Stout Memorial Hospital）被轰炸的情况。该电报于9月18日至19日午夜从香港发出，但至今未送达路透社上海办事处。

路透社香港办事处发出的该份电报原文如下：

“广州。可靠消息获悉，华南浸信会传教团位于梧州的斯托特纪念医院于9月17日遭九架日机轰炸，建筑物被五枚炸弹直接命中。美方职员无人受伤，但估计损失达15万美元。”

Japanese Censorship of Reuter
Messages Revealed

Many Details of C.N.A.C. Affair and Air Raids
In Kwangtung Held Up ; Tsingtao Wire Altered

Shanghai, Sept. 2.

FOR the information of their clients, Reuters publish herewith
the texts of various telegrams despatched by their Hongkong
Office to Shanghai, which were held up by the Japanese censors
in Shanghai. The following four telegrams were despatched during
the morning of August 24, concerning the C.N.A.C. disaster :

Hongkong 10.26 a.m.—“Chinese official sources state C.N.A.C. passenger plane from Hongkong to Wuchow with full load passengers shot down by Japanese planes Canton River Delta this morning.”

Hongkong 10.30 a.m.—“C.N.A.C. admit plane forced down claiming passengers all safe Company adds ‘international complications probably occur’ which is taken to indicate foreigners aboard plane.”

Hongkong 10.45 a.m.—“Add C.N.A.C.: No shots hit plane but number Japanese pursuits continually dived over machine forcing it lower and lower until American pilot eventually made forced landing. Authoritative circles here say attackers believed Sun Fo aboard, but it now established Sun Fo still in Hongkong, although learned number other important Chinese officials aboard.”

Hongkong 12.35 p.m. — “Official C.N.A.C. statement says, Plane forced down Yuetshing, 25 miles south-west Canton, landed shallow river, all passengers safe. Machine left Kaitak at 8.04 a.m. carrying 14 Chinese passengers, no foreigners. At 8.35 a.m. pilot wirelessed: Japanese planes pursuing —I am being forced land. At 8.38 a.m. pilot wirelessed: Succeeded landing all safe.

It appears now Sun Fo actually left for Hankow by Eurasia plane this morning, having at first intended travel C.N.A.C. plane, and it believed almost certain Japanese planes thought Sun Fo aboard C.N.A.C. machine.”

It is now also revealed that two other telegrams, despatched from Reuter’s Hongkong Office to Shanghai, were held up by the censors. Both were despatched on June 16. The texts of these two telegrams ran:

Hongkong 4.30 p.m.—“Canton. Officially claimed six unescorted Japanese bombers brought down at Lokchong near Kwangtung Hunan border this morning. It stated slow-moving crafts which engaged bombing Canton-Hankow railway were attacked by 10 swift Chinese pursuits, who flew rings around raiders, continuously machine-gunning them and crashing them one by one. Canton is elated at news and populace, feeling terrific reaction from recent bombings, going wild with joy.”

Hongkong 11 p.m.—“Canton. City this evening in state complete jubilation following official despatches carrying colourful description air battle at Lokchong. These state squadron Japanese bombers flew from Amoy, through Fukien, visiting Namhung, Szehing and Lokchong, and were surprised latter place by Chinese pursuits. Stated one raider brought down at Lienhsien, one at Kaukong, one at Mabar, three at Lokchong. The latter already located and bear numerical marks 707, 7958, 21079, together with Japanese factory marks. Machines are twin-engined heavy bombers carrying five airmen apiece. It is added that Chinese pursuits hovered at 18,000 feet awaiting raiders, then swooped giving enemy no chances, slow bombers being completely at mercy swifter Chinese pursuits.”

None of the above telegrams have been released to Reuter’s Shanghai Office, even yet, by the Japanese censors.

Copies From Hongkong

Reuters have been able to receive the texts of these telegrams only through the action of their Hongkong Office, which has now supplied copies of the telegrams as sent from Hongkong.

Incidentally, all the above telegrams were sent from Hongkong to London, where they were duly published.

Reuters also consider it their duty to their clients to inform them of another censoring incident which occurred to a telegram in transit between Reuter’s Tsingtao and Shanghai offices.

On July 7, Reuter’s Tsingtao Office despatched the following cable:
“Briton, Jock Crichton, stopped by Japanese sentry for smoking cigarette Commercial Wharf this morning. Crichton extinguished cigarette and apologized, whereupon sentry slapped his face.”

The only telegram received from Tsingtao by Reuter’s Shanghai Office on July 7 ran:
“Briton, Jock Crichton, stopped by Japanese sentry for smoking cigarette Commercial Wharf this morning. Crichton extinguished cigarette and apologized, whereupon sentry let him go.”—Reuter.

1938年9月14日

日本对路透讯息的
审查被揭露

中航事件及广东空袭的许多细节被扣留；青岛电文被篡改

上海，9月2日。

为了告知其客户，路透社特此公布由其香港办事处发往上海、但在上海被日本检查员扣留的各份电报原文。以下四份电报于8月24日上午发出，涉及中航灾难：

香港 上午10:26 — “中国官方消息来源称，今晨一架从中航香港飞往梧州、满载乘客的客机在广东三角洲被日机击落。”

香港 上午10:30 — “中航承认飞机被迫降落，声称乘客均安全。公司补充说‘可能会发生国际纠纷’，这被解读为表明机上有外国人。”

香港 上午10:45 — “补正中航消息：没有炮弹击中飞机，但多架日本战斗机不断俯冲逼近飞机，迫使飞机越来越低，直到美国飞行员最终被迫降落。此地权威人士称，攻击者认为孙佛（Sun Fo，即孙科）在机上，但现在已确定孙佛仍在香港，尽管获悉机上还有其他多名中国重要官员。”

香港 下午12:35 — “中航官方声明称，飞机在距广州西南25英里的粤兴（Yuetshing，音译）被迫降落，降落在浅河中，所有乘客安全。机器于上午8:04离开启德，载有14名中国乘客，无外国人。上午8:35飞行员发无线电报：日机追击——我被迫降落。上午8:38飞行员发无线电报：成功降落，全员安全。

现在看来，孙佛实际上已于今晨乘坐欧亚航空公司的飞机前往汉口，他起初打算乘坐中航飞机，因此几乎可以肯定日本飞机误以为孙佛在中航飞机上。”

现在还揭露，另有两份从路透社香港办事处发往上海的电报被检查员扣留。这两份电报均于6月16日发出。这两份电报的原文如下：

香港 下午4:30 — “广州。官方宣称，今晨在靠近广东湖南边界的乐昌（Lokchong，音译）击落了六架无护航的日本轰炸机。消息称，从事轰炸广州-汉口铁路的慢速飞行器遭到10架快速中国战斗机的攻击，中国战机围绕袭击者盘旋，持续用机枪扫射并逐一将其击落。广州对此消息感到欢欣鼓舞，民众因最近遭受轰炸而产生强烈反应，欣喜若狂。”

香港 晚上11:00 — “广州。今晚全城处于完全欢庆状态，原因是收到了带有生动描述乐昌空战的官方电讯。这些电讯称，一队日本轰炸机从厦门起飞，穿过福建，访问了南雄（Namhung，音译）、始兴（Szehing，音译）和乐昌，并在后者地点遭到中国战斗机的突袭。消息称，一架袭击者在连县（Lienhsien，音译）被击落，一架在高坑（Kaukong，音译），一架在马坝（Mabar，音译），三架在乐昌。后者的残骸已被找到，并带有编号标记 707, 7958, 21079，以及日本工厂标记。这些机器是双引擎重型轰炸机，每架载有五名飞行员。另补充说，中国战斗机在18,000英尺高空盘旋等待袭击者，然后俯冲攻击，使敌人毫无机会，缓慢的轰炸机完全受制于更快的中国战斗机。”

上述电报至今均未由日本检查员向路透社上海办事处发布。

来自香港的副本

路透社仅因其香港办事处的行动才得以收到这些电报的原文，该办事处现已提供从香港发出时的电报副本。

顺便提一下，上述所有电报均从香港发送至伦敦，并在那里如期发表。

路透社还认为有责任向其客户通报另一起审查事件，该事件发生在路透社青岛办事处与上海办事处之间传输的一份电报上。

7月7日，路透社青岛办事处发出了以下电报：
“英国人 Jock Crichton，今晨在商务码头吸烟时被日本哨兵拦下。Crichton 熄灭香烟并道歉，随后哨兵扇了他一记耳光。”

7月7日路透社上海办事处从青岛收到的唯一一份电报内容为：
“英国人 Jock Crichton，今晨在商务码头吸烟时被日本哨兵拦下。Crichton 熄灭香烟并道歉，随后哨兵放他走了。”—路透社。

Enquiries with reference to the information

维持与中国审查制度相同的体系

昨日从最可靠的消息来源获悉，上海诚信的商业公司今后无需将其私人密码副本存交日本检查员。

昨日在此发表的一份声明中指出，诚信商行目前的商业电报保密性将被取消，但在昨日清晨，日本人就此事与上海某些代表性商业利益集团达成了协议。

然而，当地外国商行仍需从各自的总领事馆获取身份证明书，并存交日本检查员，这一制度在中国政权时期曾实行过。据称，在开具这些证明书所需的时间内，当地诚信商行与外界的正常通讯往来不会中断。

《字林西报》代表在当天采访了几位著名银行家后获悉，上午10点左右，本地各大银行已与日本人达成协议，据此它们将继续使用

提出抗议

据悉，英美当局昨日已就有关密码电报的新规定向日本总领事馆提出抗议。据了解， respective Consuls-General 分别提出了交涉。另有报道称，英国当局还就数日前《曼彻斯特卫报》记者 J. B. Higginson 先生发给该报的电报被扣押一事提出了抗议。

在昨日下午的日本新闻发布会上，发言人承认收到了美国总领事的抗议，但表示他尚未获悉英国总领事提出的抗议。

问题已解决

据悉，私人电报不会获得与诚信商行商业电报同等的待遇，在此类情况下，有必要向检查员提供解码电报所需的手段。

“整个问题似乎至少暂时得到了解决，”一位外国银行官员昨日表示。“我们自然不赞成任何形式的审查，但达成的协议对我们来说并非不能接受。”

通过一家电报公司获悉，日本人可能保留随时要求查看秘密密码本的权利，但也补充说，他们这样做可能性很小。

一位电报公司官员将昨日在此发布的关于银行和商行使用秘密密码的新不利裁决的公告形容为“非常不幸”。他认为，此类公告可能会引起不少误解，并希望真实情况能得到最广泛的宣传。

据悉，整个困难围绕着是否要求商业公司将密码本存交日本检查员的问题。各公司自然视其密码本为极度机密事项，并补充说，任何此类要求都会引起严重的复杂情况，并导致当地商业通讯停滞。

截至昨日深夜，一切问题均已理顺，受访商行表示，他们仅是通过报纸得知所谓的变更，并未被日本人要求将密码本副本存交检查员。

THE CHINA PRESS. 29 JAN 1938
（批：clcd）

Two Protests
Filed Against
Trade Cable
Censorship

American And British
Consulates-General
Take Action

LOCAL BUSINESS
CONCERNS STIRRED

Protests Also Sent On
Held Up Messages
Of Timperley

Japanese censorship of commercial telegrams and cables started yesterday morning, brought forth two protests, one from Mr. Herbert Phillips, British Consul-General, and the other from the American Consulate-General.

At the Japanese press conference last night, the embassy spokesman admitted that he had learned that an American protest had been received but if the British protest had been filed, he had not been informed up to the time of the conference.

The filing of the British protest was confirmed at the British Consulate-General. It was also confirmed that the British Consul-General filed protests against the censorship of messages filed by Mr. H. J. Timperley, China correspondent for the Manchester Guardian.

Although the matter of commercial cable censorship was generally discussed by local business concerns yesterday, no definite action in the way of complaints was forthcoming from these quarters.

The American Chamber of Commerce, pressed with other matters in making preparations for its annual meeting, gave only passing attention to the matter since no complaints from members had been lodged.

Too Early To Predict

A spokesman of the chamber pointed out that since the censorship had been in force only one day, it was yet too early to predict what would happen.

All messages, commercial or press have been passing through the Japanese censorship office since its establishment and as far as the use of standard codes or plain language are concerned, the Nipponese have been in a position to exercise commercial cable censorship for quite some time.

It also was learned that the cable companies first became aware of censorship when it was announced by the Japanese at the press conference Thursday.

Under the regulations announced by the censors, the Japanese must be informed of the code to be used and if it is a private code, messages filed must bear a consular chop. Such messages will be accepted only from firms endorsed in writing by their respective consulates as bona-fide concerns. Concerns or persons caught practising abuses will be subject to having their filing privileges taken away.

During the censorship discussion at the press conference last night the question of press messages was raised.

Timperley Makes Inquiry

Mr. Timperley, who was present, inquired as to whether or not the Japanese authorities had received the British consular protest in connection with his recently censored messages.

The answer to this was that the spokesman had no information on the subject. He expected, however, that he could obtain information.

Correspondents also asked for the telephone number of the censors so that they might call themselves to find out whether or not their messages had been censored. The number was not available but it was promised to be made known today.

在昨晚的日本新闻发布会上，使馆发言人承认他获悉已收到美国的抗议，但如果英国已提交抗议，他在会议结束前尚未被告知。

英国总领事馆证实了英国抗议书的提交。同时也证实，英国总领事就《曼彻斯特卫报》驻华记者 H. J. Timperley 先生提交的电报受审查一事提出了抗议。

预测尚早

商会发言人指出，由于审查制度仅实施了一天，现在预测后续发展还为时过早。

自日本检查机构设立以来，所有商业或新闻电报均须经由其审查，就使用标准密码或明文而言，日本人已有相当一段时间具备实施商业电缆电报审查的能力。

廷珀莱提出询问

记者们还索要了检查员的电话号码，以便自行致电查询其电报是否受到审查。当时未能提供该号码，但承诺今日公布。

page_data.en:
CABLES IN CODE
Quite naturally there was a good deal of perturbation felt in banking and business circles on Thursday evening when it became known that an official spokesman at the Japanese press conference had announced that the Japanese authorities at present exercising functions of censorship over telegraphic communications had issued a ruling that no messages in code would be accepted for transmission unless "certified to be bona-fide commercial telegrams by the Consular official having jurisdiction over the sender of the telegram and in a code submitted to the censors at the time of filing, or previously." If such a ruling were enforced it would mean that the private codes of banks and big business firms would no longer be strictly private, that confidential transactions would have some of their confidential character destroyed. The Japanese intention, apparently, is to prevent what might appear to be ordinary coded commercial telegrams from being used as a cloak to cover the sending of military or political messages, but such a wholesale ruling as above was no doubt hurriedly and somewhat thoughtlessly framed. It would not be constructive or politic to ask banks and certain other big interests to deposit copies of their private and confidential ciphers with the censors or to get a Consular certificate every time a telegram had to be sent. Clarification came yesterday morning when it was learned that members of the Foreign Exchange Bankers Association and other foreign interests were not expected to deposit their individual private codes but would carry on as heretofore under general certificates as to bona fides. It is exactly the same system as was in force under the Chinese censorship, except that banks and foreign firms will require new certificates by reason of the fact that many of the old ones appear to have been taken away. Doubtless the Japanese reserve to themselves the right to call for code books in cases where they have cause to doubt the purpose and purport of any particular firm's messages, but that is a reasonable enough reservation. The new ruling apparently bars all Chinese firms and individuals from using coded telegrams, but this is one of those precautionary penalties which de facto control brought about by force of arms would consider itself justified in imposing. What appeared at first to be so drastic a measure has been found on explanation to be little more than a formality under the new conditions, and so Shanghai breathes freely again.
page_data.zh:
密码电报
周四晚间，当得知日本新闻发布会的一位官方发言人宣布，目前行使电报通信审查职能的日本当局已发布一项裁决，除非“由对发报人拥有管辖权的领事官员证明为真实的商业电报，并使用在提交时或此前已向审查员备案的密码”，否则不接受任何密码电报进行传输，银行界和商界自然感到相当不安。如果执行此类裁决，将意味着银行和大型商行的私人密码不再严格保密，机密交易的保密性将受到一定程度的破坏。日本的意图显然是为了防止看似普通的密码商业电报被用作掩护，以发送军事或政治信息，但上述这种一刀切的裁决无疑是在匆忙且略显轻率的情况下制定的。要求银行和某些其他大型利益集团将其私密且机密的密码副本存放在审查员处，或者每次发送电报时都获取领事证书，既无建设性也不明智。昨天上午情况得到澄清，据悉外汇银行家协会成员及其他外国利益方无需存放其各自的私人密码，而是可以像以前一样，凭关于真实性的总证书继续运作。这与中方审查制度下实行的体系完全相同，只不过由于许多旧证书似乎已被收回，银行和外国公司需要新的证书。毫无疑问，日本保留在怀疑任何特定公司的电报目的和主旨时要求查看密码本的权利，但这是一种足够合理的保留。新的规定显然禁止所有中国公司和个人使用密码电报，但这属于凭借武力造成的事实控制认为有权施加的预防性惩罚之一。起初看来如此严厉的措施，经解释后发现不过是在新条件下的一种形式而已，因此上海再次松了一口气。

SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE
S. B. REGISTRY
No. S. B. D. 2398
Date 10 / 1 38

January 8, 1938.

Journal de Shanghai :-

THE JAPANESE CENSORSHIP IN SHANGHAI

On November 20 last year, Domei, the official Japanese news agency, sent out the following note to newspapers in Shanghai :-
"The Japanese control along the Lower Yangtze up to Soochow has dealt a most vital blow to the Chinese censorship of telegrams and radio messages.
"The management of the foreign cable companies has declared to a representative of Domei that as soon as the occupation of Soochow became known, the Chinese censors 'disappeared' from the telegraph and radio offices in the Settlement.
"The censorship has been in force in Shanghai since 1930. It was bete noire with foreign Press correspondents, because of unjustified cuts and unauthorized alterations of messages.
"The foreign Consular authorities have on many occasions declared that censorship in the Settlement was incompatible with the Treaties, but the cable companies, threatened with a loss of their business in the interior if they did not submit to the Chinese demands, were obliged to accept the censorship."
Thus, on November 20, the Japanese admitted the Chinese censorship of telegrams sent abroad was illegal, that the Consular authorities regarded it as contrary to the Treaties and that it was imposed on the foreign cable companies by means of threats only. Furthermore, the Japanese authorities have never permitted the Chinese to censor Japanese telegrams in the International Settlement.
Now, on January 6, 1938, the Japanese authorities, claiming as successors to the Chinese Government in the International Settlement, placed Japanese censors in the cable companies for the purpose of censoring telegrams sent abroad.
There is no better condemnation of the Japanese action than the declaration issued by Domei on November 20 last year.
If the Japanese authorities, in establishing an illegal censorship, plead war emergency and the necessity of assuring the safety of their armies, one can admit that it is a case of force majeure. The Japanese authorities, however, have presented themselves as successors to the Chinese Government. But one cannot lay claim to any property not legally possessed by the person from whom one inherits.
As regards the censorship of telegrams, a distinction should be made between messages destined for the interior of China and those for abroad. When the Japanese censor Chinese telegrams they are exercising a right belonging to the Chinese Government. In the case

1938年1月8日。

《上海日报》（Journal de Shanghai）：

上海的日本审查制度

去年11月20日，日本官方通讯社同盟社向上海各报社发出如下说明：
“日本对直至苏州的下扬子江地区的控制，对中文电报和无线电信息的审查制度给予了最致命的打击。
“外国电缆公司管理层向同盟社代表声明，一旦苏州被占领的消息传开，中国审查员便从租界的电报局和无线电局‘消失’了。
“自1930年以来，上海一直实行审查制度。由于无故删减和擅自更改信息，该制度成为外国新闻通讯员的眼中钉。
“外国领事当局曾多次声明，租界内的审查制度与条约不符，但电缆公司因担心若不顺从中方要求将失去内地业务，被迫接受审查。”
因此，在11月20日，日本承认对中国发出的外洋电报进行审查是非法的，领事当局视其为违反条约，且这仅是通过威胁手段强加给外国电缆公司的。此外，日本当局从未允许中国人在国际租界内审查日本电报。
现在，在1938年1月6日，日本当局自称是国际租界内中国政府的继承者，在电缆公司派驻日本审查员，以审查发出的外洋电报。
对于日本此举，没有比同盟社去年11月20日发表的声明更好的谴责了。
如果日本当局在建立非法审查制度时，以战争紧急状态和确保军队安全的必要性为借口，人们可以承认这是不可抗力。然而，日本当局将自己呈现为中国政府的继承者。但是，一个人不能声称拥有其继承人所不合法拥有的任何财产。
关于电报审查，应区分发往中国内地的信息和发往国外的信息。当日本人审查中国电报时，他们是在行使属于中国政府的权利。在

January 8, 1938. - 2 -

of telegrams for abroad sent out from the International
Settlement, it is a different matter altogether for we
have just demonstrated that the Chinese right, not
founded on law, cannot be validly invoked by the Japanese
to-day.
There remains the plea of military
exigencies, the only plausible plea. The Japanese
spokesman has already made reference to it.. The reason
given by the Japanese authorities for the censorship
is that the present abnormal situation in the Foreign
Settlements and the fact that the terrorist outrages
could have been ordered by messages received from the
interior. This censorship, he said, is necessary for
the safety of the Japanese Army. One of the journalists
present then asked whether the spokesman could give an
assurance that all telegrams of a political nature signed
by accredited correspondents with the Japanese authorities
would not be censored, as these journalists could not be
suspected of furnishing military information to the
Chinese Government and much less with being mixed up
in terrorist attempts. The spokesman replied, saying that
it all depended on circumstances.
Thus,. the spokesman justified the censorship
above all by the necessity of putting a stop to terrorist
outrages.
We will go further. We admit that the
Japanese military authorities, as any other military
authorities, in time of war, have to guard the secret
of their operations, their plans, their strength, the
movements of their troops. To preserve the secrecy
of their military operations and the safety of their
troops are the only two reasons by which the Japanese,
in times of war, can justify their censorship.
In that case, they cannot hold the right
of censorship from the Chinese Government for the latter
never had the right to exercise it; they can hold the
right from the International Settlement. In fact, it is
only the International Settlement which has the right
to authorize the Japanese, by reason of the state of war,
to keep a watch on telegrams.
Such a censorship, because of the
exceptional circumstances, should be carried out with
intelligence and consideration. A censorship that is
unfair and stupid would be absolutely intolerable.
Bullying should not be permitted. A telegram should not
be held up for hours on the ground that there are
insufficient censors or that they are not very familiar
with foreign languages or that they are incapable of
deciding whether the messages are really harmful to the
safety of the Japanese Army. They should not confuse
political comments with military questions.
When a censorship is instituted in one's
country, it is little liked; but when it is instituted
in another country it is doubly disliked. Every measure
should be taken to cause as little trouble as possible.
Censorship is a difficult work; it requires tact.

G.M.

从国际租界发出的外洋电报方面，情况则完全不同，因为我们刚刚论证，缺乏法律依据的中国权利，如今不能被日本有效援引。
剩下的只有军事急需这一理由，这也是唯一看似合理的理由。日本发言人已经提到了这一点。日本当局给出的审查理由是，外国租界目前的异常局势，以及恐怖暴行可能是由来自内地的信息下令实施的。他说，这种审查对于日军的安全是必要的。当时在场的一名记者询问，发言人能否保证所有由经日本当局认证的特派记者签署的政治性质电报不受审查，因为这些记者不可能被怀疑向中国政府提供军事情报，更不可能卷入恐怖企图。发言人回答说，这完全取决于具体情况。
因此，发言人主要通过制止恐怖暴行的必要性来为上述审查辩护。
我们将进一步阐述。我们承认，日本军事当局同任何其他军事当局一样，在战时必须保守其行动、计划、兵力及部队调动之秘密。保守军事行动的秘密和保障部队安全，是日本在战时为其审查制度辩护的唯一两个理由。
在这种情况下，他们不能从中国政府那里获得审查权，因为后者从未拥有行使该权利的权力；他们只能从国际租界获得该权利。事实上，只有国际租界有权因战争状态授权日本监视电报。
鉴于特殊情况，此类审查应以智慧和体谅的方式执行。不公平且愚蠢的审查是绝对无法容忍的。不应允许欺凌行为。不应以审查员不足、不熟悉外语或无法判断信息是否真的危害日军安全为由，将电报扣留数小时。他们不应将政治评论与军事问题混淆。
在本国实施审查时，人们尚且不太喜欢；而在他国实施时，厌恶之情则加倍。应采取一切措施，尽可能减少麻烦。审查是一项困难的工作，需要讲究策略。

G.M.

such for objective impediments
free flow of news from the
Far East. British, French, German
minds are trained along similar
lines to our own; but when it
is the Orient that is being
handled by Western correspondents
and editors, we are faced with a
subtler problem. The Oriental
viewpoint, with its traditions or al-
liances with Western interests, per-
sonalities which enter into this mat-
ter, of course, is far more difficult to
state than the mere majority of
foreign correspondents in the Far
East. Furthermore, the representative
British and American organizations
are free from any other than a tem-
porary and passing desire to tell us
that part of the story.

**Real Difficulties Inevitable**

On the other hand, there are a
number of very real difficulties.
News agencies such as the British
Agency (Reuter), the French Trans-
ocean Agency, and the China News
Agency, which have their offices in
nationalistic centers like Paris, London
or the treaty ports of China, have in
the Far East itself it is difficult to
believe that their dispatches carry a
similar bias. Japanese news
agencies of course are notoriously
and aggressively nationalistic. Reu-
ter's, on the other hand, actually the
most reliable of all, works on
a rule in close harmony with British
officialdom, and endeavours to keep on
good terms also with the big foreign
business firms in China, from whom
it derives a handsome profit through
the sale of telegraphic market re-
ports.

Although the Associated Press and
United Press have close working
arrangements with officially control-
led news agencies both in China and
Japan, American news-gathering
organizations usually are credited
with a fair measure of objectivity.
But here again certain independ-
ables must be taken into account.
Most news agencies, it must be re-
membered, are concerned primarily
with the sale of news on a wholesale
basis to newspapers, which then re-
tail it to their readers. As in any
business, it is the retail customer,
in the last analysis, whose predilec-
tions determine the character of the
news with which he is supplied. Big
profits cannot be made without big
circulation, and a big circulation
cannot be built up unless the public
is given what the majority of the
public wants.

What does the public want? Riegel,
in his searching analysis of Na-
tionalism and its effects upon the
corruption of news, points out that
large circulation demand "hot"
news; that is, news that is printed
immediately after the event occurs
is more or less superficial or sensa-
tional.

Large circulations also demand
new and unusual matter that is
pleasant reading for the masses of
population. The result has been that
American newspapers have curried
the editor's favor in the speed
and quantity of their news reports
and in "dressing up" the news so as
to best catch the eye of the mob.

**"Remote Control" Cited**

Any American news agency corre-
spondent in the Far East could
produce from his files half a dozen
telegrams proving the truth of these
statements. "New York says rush
colorful details stressing 'American
angle' is a typical instruction, and
if there are no colorful details and
no American angle the correspond-
ent has to choose between thinking
up some himself or having some

bright young man in the New York
office do so on his behalf.

This system of "remote control"
leads inevitably to distortion and
misrepresentation of facts; what
starts off from the Far East as a
good honest beefsteak often finds
itself dished up at the other end
as an unrecognizable goulash. Now
and then an organization overreaches
itself in the effort to sharpen the
features of a situation which may
be in fact quite nebulous. Thus in
1932 an American agency which had
prematurely announced the opening
of the Japanese army's campaign
for the subjugation of Jehol, was
obliged to invent a snow blizzard to
explain to its readers why operations
had been suddenly "halted."

These contributory shortcomings
on the part of American news-
papers and magazines have been
emphasized only because they pre-
sent the most obvious example of
the way in which news is affected by
the economic, political and de-
mand. This might be
ameliorated somewhat if the cen-
sorship and other restrictions which
now clog the news-gathering ma-
chinery were to be removed and if,
in addition, there could be a sub-
stantial reduction in cable tolls on
news dispatches from the Far East.
In theory at least, a great deal of
the "writing up" which now takes
place at the receiving end would be
eliminated if the correspondent were
in a position to amplify messages
which often, under present con-
ditions, must be cut to the proverbial
bone. But it is doubtful whether
much real progress toward the dis-
semination of objective truth can be
achieved until the public at large
has been educated up to the point
of preferring the significant to the
sensational.

Ed.'s note: As we (Pacific Affairs)
go to press, a letter from the author
of the above article is received,
throwing a somewhat different light
on censorship developments within
recent months. A correspondent in
Tokyo during the last four days in
February filed 8,500 words, of which
half were suppressed. "This" — to
quote the correspondent — "was an
exceptional instance, but per-
haps it should be noted ... More-
over, under the martial law regime
which has been in force here for
nearly a month now, the restrictions
on the local press, both as to news

matter and pictures, have been much
more rigorous than normally."
The author, who is now in Shang-
hai, adds that he found the Chinese
censorship is conducted much more
intelligently, correspondents being
notified by telephone in the event of
their messages being censored.

14827

此类客观障碍阻碍了来自远东的新闻自由流通。英国人、法国人、德国人的思维训练方式与我们相似；但当西方记者和编辑处理东方事务时，我们面临着一个更为微妙的问题。当然，东方的观点，连同其传统或与西方利益的联盟、卷入此事的人物性格，比仅仅列举在远东的大多数外国记者要难以陈述得多。此外，具有代表性的英美机构除了有一种暂时且短暂的愿望向我们讲述那部分故事外，不受任何其他因素左右。

**不可避免的切实困难**

另一方面，存在许多非常现实的困难。像英国通讯社（路透社）、法国跨洋通讯社和中国新闻社这样的新闻机构，其办事处设在巴黎、伦敦或中国条约口岸等民族主义中心，很难相信它们在远东本身发出的电讯带有类似的偏见。日本新闻机构当然是出了名地且具有攻击性的民族主义。另一方面，路透社实际上是所有机构中最可靠的，其运作规则与英国官方保持密切和谐，并努力与中国的大型外国商业公司保持良好关系，通过出售电报市场报告从中获取丰厚利润。

尽管美联社和合众社与中国和日本官方控制的新闻机构有着密切的工作安排，但美国的新闻采集组织通常被认为具有相当程度的客观性。但在此必须考虑到某些独立变量。必须记住，大多数新闻机构主要关心的是以批发方式向报纸出售新闻，然后报纸再将其零售给读者。正如在任何商业中一样，归根结底，是零售客户的偏好决定了供应给他的新闻的性质。没有巨大的发行量就无法获得巨额利润，除非向公众提供大多数公众想要的东西，否则无法建立巨大的发行量。

公众想要什么？里格尔（Riegel）在对民族主义及其对新闻腐败的影响进行的深入分析中指出，大发行量需要“热点”新闻；也就是说，在事件发生后立即印刷的新闻或多或少是肤浅或耸人听闻的。

大发行量还需要新颖且不寻常的内容，以供广大民众愉悦阅读。结果，美国报纸为了最好地吸引大众的眼球，在新闻报道的速度和数量以及“包装”新闻方面迎合了编辑的喜好。

**引用“远程控制”**

任何在远东的美国新闻机构记者都能从他的档案中拿出半打电报来证明这些陈述的真实性。“纽约说赶紧提供强调‘美国角度’的生动的细节”是一条典型的指令，如果没有生动的细节和美国角度，记者就必须在自行编造一些内容，或者让纽约办公室里的一些聪明的年轻人代劳之间做出选择。

这种“远程控制”体系不可避免地导致事实的扭曲和误传；从远东出发时原本是一块优质诚实的牛排，到了另一端往往被端上来变成了一锅无法辨认的杂烩炖肉。偶尔，一个机构在试图 sharpen（突出/锐化）实际上可能相当模糊的局势特征时用力过猛。因此，在1932年，一家美国通讯社过早地宣布了日军征服热河战役的开始，不得不编造一场暴风雪，向其读者解释为何行动突然“停止”。

强调美国报纸和杂志的这些辅助性缺陷，仅仅是因为它们提供了新闻受经济、政治和需求影响方式的最明显例子。如果目前阻碍新闻采集机制的检查制度和其他限制得以解除，并且此外，来自远东的新闻电讯的电报费用能大幅降低，这种情况或许会有所改善。至少在理论上，如果记者能够扩充那些在目前条件下往往必须删减到极致的讯息，那么目前在接收端发生的大量“润色写作”将被消除。但是，在广大公众被教育到倾向于重视有意义而非耸人听闻的内容之前，能否在传播客观真理方面取得多少真正进展，是值得怀疑的。

编者注：当我们（《太平洋事务》）付印时，收到了上述文章作者的一封信，对最近几个月检查制度的发展提供了略有不同的视角。二月份最后四天在东京的一位记者发送了8,500字，其中一半被删禁。“这”——引用该记者的话——“是一个例外情况，但或许应当指出……此外，在这里已实施近一个月的戒严体制下，当地新闻界在新闻内容和图片方面的限制比平时严格得多。”目前身处上海的作者补充说，他发现中国的审查工作执行得更为明智，如果记者的电讯被审查，会通过电话通知他们。

Timperley Writes On Censorship

Pacific Affairs Article
Declares China's
Cause Right

(The following article "Makers of Public Opinion About the Far East" appears in the June issue of Pacific Affairs, quarterly magazine published by the Institute of Pacific Relations.—Editor.)

By H. J. TIMPERLEY

Among the factors which help to form public opinion about the Far East one of the most important is the news of dispatches which flow day by day or cable from correspondents and news agency men in those stationed in China and Japan. While it is realized that a correspondent of the Associated Press, Reuter, Tass, Havas, Domei, etc., represents a cross section of world opinion, yet his articles have still wide circulation. It will be seen that here lies a field that can work with tremendous potency for either good or evil in the field of international relations.

News-gathering conditions in the two countries vary greatly, yet certain problems are common to each. There is, for instance, the language barrier which effectively shuts off all but a very small minority of correspondents from primary sources of information. Japanese is one of the world's most difficult languages and it is doubtful whether a foreign correspondent, fully qualified in other respects, has ever been able to read and use it with any ease or fluency. As a result not only does he depend upon native translators for his knowledge of what is published in the Japanese press and, however loyal and capable the translator, it is questionable whether he will at any time very completely his employer's more objective view as to what should properly be translated.

Etiquette, which demands no evidence of open offense to the foreign office, plus a patriotic desire to present his country in the best possible light, may well combine to set up in the mind of an otherwise well-intentioned translator a sort of subconscious censorship which obscures the facts. In China the position is not greatly different. The number of professional correspondents who have reached the point of being able to interview a Chinese official in his own language is extremely small, and difficulty of reading signs and newspapers is complicated by the fact that many of them are still written in the classical language which even a native is able to master only after many years of study.

Rigorous Training For Job

It is difficult to see how this situation could be remedied unless those responsible who could afford it were to send to their Far Eastern correspondents who had just been given an opportunity to study the language and culture of the country for a period of two or three years before taking up his job. Such an expense might be justified in some cases as expensive correspondence bears fruit. Only when they are thoroughly trained as far as possible governments would do a highly informed corps of Far Eastern specialists in this way and so, to some extent, do away with the lack of foreign commercial understanding.

There is no reason why a wealthy newspaper or news agency should not adopt the same method. Under the present system correspondents are sent out with little or no training. No official is placed upon his movements as a rule, but lack of telegraphic facilities often produce the same result. Thus in Japan the foreign correspondent who steps off the boat, puts on his news is hampered by hostile wording of his press messages.

But such situations both in China and in Japan tend to make it difficult for the correspondent to get at the truth. No official is placed upon his movements as a rule, but lack of telegraphic facilities often produce the same result. Thus in Japan the foreign correspondent who steps off the boat, puts on his news is hampered by hostile wording of his press messages.

They state that they write what they like and censor it themselves. This statement is made with less than full truth. Correspondents in Japan are not allowed to write what they like. They must submit their copy to the censors. If they do not, they are liable to be expelled. The censors are not always reasonable. They often delete passages which are perfectly harmless. They also sometimes allow passages which are definitely misleading. The result is that the foreign correspondent in Japan is never quite sure what he can say and what he cannot. He is always walking on eggshells.

In China a different but equally difficult situation prevails. Here the censorship is less rigid but more unpredictable. The authorities are anxious to present China in a favorable light to the outside world. They therefore encourage correspondents to write favorably about China. But they also insist that nothing should be written which might harm China's interests. This means that correspondents are often prevented from writing the truth about conditions in China. They are forced to paint a rosy picture which does not correspond to reality.

The result of all this is that the public in the West gets a distorted view of the Far East. They do not know what is really happening in China and Japan. They are misled by the censorship and by the self-censorship of the correspondents. This is a serious matter because public opinion in the West has a great influence on the policies of the Western governments towards the Far East. If public opinion is based on false information, then the policies will be wrong.

What can be done to remedy this situation? One suggestion is that the governments of China and Japan should relax their censorship and allow correspondents to write freely. Another suggestion is that the correspondents themselves should resist the pressure to conform and should strive to tell the truth even if it is unpleasant. A third suggestion is that the public in the West should be more critical of the news they receive from the Far East and should try to get information from other sources.

Ultimately the solution lies in the hands of the correspondents themselves. They must realize that their duty is to tell the truth and not to serve the interests of any particular government. They must be courageous enough to stand up for the truth even if it means risking their jobs or their safety. Only then can they hope to earn the respect of their readers and to make a real contribution to the understanding of the Far East.

廷珀利论新闻审查

《太平洋事务》文章
宣称中国事业正义

（以下文章“关于远东的舆论制造者”刊登于国际关系学会出版的季刊《太平洋事务》六月号。——编者按。）

H. J. 廷珀利 著

在有助于形成关于远东舆论的各种因素中，最重要的因素之一是从驻中国和日本的记者及通讯社人员那里日复一日通过信函或电报发回的新闻报道。虽然人们认识到，美联社、路透社、塔斯社、哈瓦斯社、同盟社等机构的记者代表了世界舆论的一个横截面，但他们的文章仍然广泛流传。可以看出，这里存在一个领域，它能在国际关系领域产生巨大的良性或恶性影响。

两国的新闻采集条件大相径庭，但也有一些共同的问题。例如，语言障碍有效地将除极少数记者以外的所有人隔绝在主要信息来源之外。日语是世界上最难学的语言之一，令人怀疑是否有在其他方面完全合格的外国记者能够轻松或流利地阅读和使用它。因此，他不仅依赖本地翻译来了解日本报刊上发表的内容，而且无论翻译多么忠诚和能干，都值得怀疑他是否在任何时候都能完全贯彻其雇主对于什么应当被恰当翻译的更客观的看法。

礼节要求不得对外务省表现出公开的冒犯，加上希望以最好的形象展示本国的爱国愿望，这很可能在一个原本善意的翻译心中建立起一种潜意识的审查机制，从而掩盖事实。在中国的情况并无太大不同。能够达到用中文直接采访中国官员水平的职业记者人数极少，而阅读招牌和报纸的困难又因许多文字仍采用文言文这一事实而变得复杂，即使是本地人也需要经过多年学习才能掌握。

严格的职业训练

很难看出这种情况如何能得到改善，除非那些有能力负担费用的责任方派遣其远东记者在正式上任前，有机会对该国的语言和文化进行为期两三年的学习。在某些情况下，这种开支可能是合理的，因为昂贵的通讯报道能带来成果。只有当他们尽可能接受全面训练时，各国政府才能以这种方式组建一支知识渊博的远东专家队伍，从而在一定程度上消除外国商业理解的缺失。

富有的报社或通讯社没有理由不采用同样的方法。在现行制度下，记者被派往海外时几乎未受任何训练。通常并没有官方人员监视他们的行动，但电报设施的缺乏往往产生相同的结果。因此，在日本，刚下船的外国记者在发布新闻时，其新闻电文常因措辞敌对而受到阻碍。

但是，在中国和日本，这样的情况都使记者难以探求真相。通常并没有官方人员监视他们的行动，但电报设施的缺乏往往产生相同的结果。因此，在日本，刚下船的外国记者在发布新闻时，其新闻电文常因措辞敌对而受到阻碍。

他们声称自己写想写的内容，并自行进行审查。这种说法并不完全属实。在日本的记者不被允许随意写作。他们必须将稿件提交给审查员。如果不这样做，他们可能会被驱逐出境。审查员并不总是讲道理的。他们经常删除完全无害的段落。有时他们也允许明显具有误导性的段落通过。结果是，在日本的外国记者永远无法确定什么可以说，什么不可以说。他总是如履薄冰。

在中国，盛行着一种不同但同样困难的局面。这里的审查制度不那么严格，但更不可预测。当局急于向外界展示中国的有利形象。因此，他们鼓励记者撰写有利于中国的报道。但他们也坚持不得撰写任何可能损害中国利益的内容。这意味着记者往往被阻止如实报道中国的情况。他们被迫描绘一幅与现实不符的美好图景。

所有这一切的结果是，西方公众对远东产生了扭曲的看法。他们不知道中国和日本真正发生了什么。他们被审查制度和记者的自我审查所误导。这是一件严重的事情，因为西方公众舆论对西方政府对远东的政策有着巨大影响。如果公众舆论基于虚假信息，那么政策就会出错。

能做些什么来改善这种情况呢？一个建议是中国和日本政府应放松审查，允许记者自由写作。另一个建议是记者本身应抵制顺从的压力，即使真相令人不快，也要努力讲述真相。第三个建议是西方公众应对从远东收到的新闻持更多批判态度，并尝试从其他来源获取信息。

最终，解决方案掌握在记者自己手中。他们必须意识到，他们的职责是讲述真相，而不是为任何特定政府的利益服务。他们必须有足够的勇气捍卫真相，即使这意味着冒着失去工作或安全的风险。只有这样，他们才有希望赢得读者的尊重，并为理解远东做出真正的贡献。

（批注：档案 30/6）

SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE
S. B. INDUSTRY
S. B. D. 2398
D.C. (CRIME) 31/ 5/ 35

May 31, 1935. Afternoon Translation.

Journal de Shanghai (May 30) :-

REQUIRED : A SCHOOL FOR CENSORS.

The "China Weekly Review" has been conducting a bitter campaign to bring about the placing of the Japanese cable between Shanghai and Nagasaki under the control of Chinese censorship, as have been the Eastern Telegraph and the Northern Telegraph.

We have preferred rather to strive for decency and for common sense as against the illegality of the censorship established in the foreign Settlements and we have protested against the violation of the right of extraterritoriality of which the censors are guilty. We have also criticised their regrettable inefficiency and disconcerting incompetency.

The Chinese censors deem it advisable to emphasize their severity rather than their misdeeds. These sorry gentlemen who, without any preparation, have been in one day placed with the various foreign telegraph offices, are too ignorant of their new work to be able to discern what "Article 26 of the International Telegraph Agreement" permits them to cut out from the telegrams handed in by the correspondents of the foreign newspapers and news agencies. They tremble unceasingly at the thought lest a phrase which, they very often do not understand or a comment the meaning of which is generally unintelligible to them should attract the attention of one of the officials of their Legations at Paris or London or Washington or Rome or Moscow and who may report the matter to Nanking, resulting in a reprimand being brought upon their heads.

These censors also deem it convenient to suppress anything that they do not understand. Most subjects are beyond them; some cause them fright. Should you use the name of Chiang Kai Shek even for the purpose of praising the Chinese Generalissimo, they hasten to stop your telegram for fear, doubtless, that the praise is inadequate.

Should you speak of incidents in the demilitarized zone and should you say that the Japanese are accusing General Yu Sue Tchong of arming the volunteers, your dispatch will be suppressed. Be it noted that you have not in any way accused Yu Sue Tchong of having supplied the volunteers with arms and ammunition; you are simply reporting that such an accusation is being made against him by the Japanese, although you can read this report in all Chinese newspapers. Nevertheless, the censor at the Eastern Telegraph Company will not allow you to cable it abroad. You should write that Yu Sue Tchong and the Japanese are the best of friends. If, after one month, Yu Sue Tchong is obliged to remove to Paotingfu, you should not say that this had been done on the orders of Nanking with the object of averting fresh trouble with the Kwantung Army, but that Yu Sue Tchong, who is the Governor of Hopei, had removed to a town located 200 kilometres to the south of the demilitarized zone simply because the climate of this locality is more suitable to the health

《上海日报》（5月30日）：-

所需者：审查员培训学校。

《密勒氏评论报》一直在开展激烈的运动，旨在促使上海与长崎之间的日本电报线路像东方电报公司和北方电报公司那样，置于中国审查制度的控制之下。

我们更倾向于努力维护体面与常识，以对抗在外国租界内建立的非法审查制度，并且我们已抗议审查员所犯下的侵犯治外法权的行为。我们也批评了他们令人遗憾的低效和令人不安的无能。

中国审查员认为，强调其严厉程度比掩盖其不当行为更为可取。这些可怜的先生们在毫无准备的情况下，一天之内就被安插到各个外国电报局，他们对新工作太过无知，无法辨别“国际电报协议第26条”允许他们从外国报纸记者和新闻通讯社提交的电报中删减哪些内容。他们不停地颤抖，唯恐某句他们往往不懂的话，或某个其含义通常令他们难以理解的评论，会引起他们在巴黎、伦敦、华盛顿、罗马或莫斯科的公使馆中某位官员的注意，而该官员可能会将此事报告给南京，导致他们受到申斥。

这些审查员还认为，删压任何他们不理解的内容是方便的。大多数主题都超出了他们的理解范围；有些甚至令他们恐惧。即使你使用蒋介石的名字是为了赞扬这位中国委员长，他们也会急忙扣留你的电报，无疑是因为担心这种赞扬不够充分。

如果你谈及非军事区的事件，并说日本人指责于学忠将军武装志愿人员，你的电讯将被扣压。请注意，你并没有以任何方式指控于学忠向志愿人员提供武器弹药；你只是报道日本人对他提出了此类指控，尽管你可以在所有中文报纸上读到这一报道。然而，东方电报公司的审查员不会允许你将其发往国外。你应该写道，于学忠和日本人是最好的朋友。如果一个月后，于学忠被迫迁往保定府，你不应该说这是奉南京之命，旨在避免与关东军发生新的麻烦，而应该说，身为河北省主席的于学忠迁往位于非军事区以南200公里的一个城镇，仅仅是因为当地的气候更有利于健康

You should never use the name of Hu Han
Min in your dispatches because the censor will turn
pale at the sight of these three words for they recall
the existence of an Opposition in China. In the view
of the censor, there is no Opposition in China. Should
Hu Han Min rejoin the Nanking Government, you will not
be permitted to report the fact immediately abroad for
it will be necessary to allow the censors a few days to
accustom themselves to the idea of not deleting the
name of Hu Han Min any more. And even then, he will
permit you only to speak of the arrival of the leader
in the capital and not of his rejoining, for this would
constitute an admission that at one time an influential
leader of the Kuomintang had thought that all was not
well. In the eyes of the censor, everything is perfect.
For him, the communists have already all been exterminated
even though, despite this, he leaves you the right to
announce every day the fresh defeats they are sustaining.
Once again, we would like to say that here
we are only referring to the misdeeds of the censors who
sin, not with the intention of doing harm to others, but
simply through ignorance and timidity.
Then there is also the reckless censor, as
ignorant as the first kind, but less scrupulous. He
thinks it will be sufficient to cut out phrases in a
haphazard way. He plays at censoring like a child
playing at being a soldier or a detective.
The "China Weekly" has reproduced a part
of the criticism which we had written recently about the
censorship from the point of view of International Law.
To-day, we are rather treating this matter from the
practical point of view. The "Review" has adopted the
role of champion of equality. "Since," says the Weekly,
"Europeans and Americans have to submit to censorship,
why should not the Japanese submit?" The paper then
demands that the Shanghai-Nagasaki telegraph should be
made to submit to censorship.
We have already expressed our views on
this subject. The Chinese censorship being absolutely
illegal, the Japanese are right not to submit. It is
up to the Europeans and the Americans to uphold respect
for their rights and to recall, among others, the terms
of the Washington Pact.
Nevertheless, if a Reuter's dispatch can
be believed, the Japanese authorities have consented to
discuss the question of the censorship of the Shanghai-
Nagasaki Cable with the Chinese Ministry of Foreign
Affairs.
After all, Sino-Japanese rapprochement
calls for some semblance of sacrifice on the part of
Japan. We say "semblance of sacrifice" advisedly,
because, whatever may be the official terms of the
future accord, everybody knows perfectly that the
censorship will not greatly trouble the Japanese
newspapermen. With them, it is a question of "face".
They will be assured that, if there are to be any censors,
they will be very obliging ones.
For our part, we do not ask for obliging
censors but censors who are at least intelligent and truly
competent. Those which are undertaking the censorship at
present understand nothing about their work. We demand
that a special school for censors be established and that
these censors be sent there.
G. M.

May 31, 1935. Afternoon Translation.

Journal de Shanghai (May 30) :-

REQUIRED : A SCHOOL FOR CENSORS.

The "China Weekly Review" has been conducting a bitter campaign to bring about the placing of the Japanese cable between Shanghai and Nagasaki under the control of Chinese censorship, as have been the Eastern Telegraph and the Northern Telegraph.

We have preferred rather to strive for decency and for common sense as against the illegality of the censorship established in the foreign Settlements and we have protested against the violation of the right of extraterritoriality of which the censors are guilty. We have also criticised their regrettable inefficiency and disconcerting incompetency.

The Chinese censors deem it advisable to emphasize their severity rather than their misdeeds. These sorry gentlemen who, without any preparation, have been in one day placed with the various foreign telegraph offices are too ignorant of their new work to be able to discern what "Article 26 of the International Telegraph Agreement" permits them to cut out from the telegrams handed in by the correspondents of the foreign newspapers and news agencies. They tremble unceasingly at the thought lest a phrase which, they very often do not understand or a comment the meaning of which is generally unintelligible to them should attract the attention of one of the officials of their Legations at Paris or London or Washington or Rome or Moscow and who may report the matter to Nanking, resulting in a reprimand being brought upon their heads.

These censors also deem it convenient to suppress anything that they do not understand. Most subjects are beyond them; some cause them fright. Should you use the name of Chiang Kai Shek even for the purpose of praising the Chinese Generalissimo, they hasten to stop your telegram for fear, doubtless, that the praise is inadequate.

Should you speak of incidents in the demilitarized zone and should you say that the Japanese are accusing General Yu Sue Tchong of arming the volunteers, your dispatch will be suppressed. Be it noted that you have not in any way accused Yu Sue Tchong of having supplied the volunteers with arms and ammunition; you are simply reporting that such an accusation is being made against him by the Japanese, though you can read this report in all Chinese newspapers. Nevertheless, the censor at the Eastern Telegraph Company will not allow you to cable it abroad. You should write that Yu Sue Tchong and the Japanese are the best of friends. If, after one month, Yu Sue Tchong is obliged to remove to Paotingfu, you should not say that this had been done on the orders of Nanking with the object of averting fresh trouble with the Kwantung Army, but that Yu Sue Tchong, who is the Governor of Hopei, had removed to a town located 200 kilometres to the south of the demilitarized zone simply because the climate of this locality is more suitable to the health

《上海日报》（5月30日）：-

要求：设立检查员学校。

《密勒氏评论报》（China Weekly Review）一直开展激烈的运动，促使连接上海与长崎的日本电缆像大北电报公司和大东电报公司的电缆一样，置于中国审查制度的控制之下。

我们更愿意努力争取体面与常识，以对抗在外国租界内建立的非法审查制度，并且我们已抗议检查员所犯下的侵犯治外法权之行为。我们也批评了他们令人遗憾的低效和令人困惑的无能。

中国检查员认为，强调其严厉性而非其劣迹更为可取。这些可怜的先生们在毫无准备的情况下，一天之内就被安置在各个外国电报局，他们对新工作知之甚少，无法辨别“《国际电报公约》第26条”允许他们从外国报纸和通讯社记者提交的电报中删减哪些内容。他们不断颤抖，唯恐某句他们往往不理解的话，或某个其含义通常令他们难以捉摸的评论，会引起其驻巴黎、伦敦、华盛顿、罗马或莫斯科公使馆中某位官员的注意，进而向南京报告，导致他们受到申斥。

这些检查员还认为，删去任何他们不理解的内容是方便的。大多数主题都超出了他们的理解范围；有些甚至令他们恐惧。即使你使用蒋介石的名字是为了赞扬这位中国总司令，他们也会急忙扣留你的电报，无疑是因为担心赞扬得不够充分。

如果你谈及非军事区的事件，并说日本人指责于学忠将军武装义勇军，你的电文将被扣押。请注意，你并未以任何方式指控于学忠向义勇军提供武器弹药；你只是报道日本人正对他提出此类指控，尽管你可以在所有中文报纸上读到这一报道。然而，大东电报公司的检查员不会允许你将其发往国外。你应该写道，于学忠和日本人是最好的朋友。如果一个月后，于学忠被迫迁往保定府，你不应该说这是奉南京之命，旨在避免与关东军发生新的麻烦，而应说，身为河北省主席的于学忠迁往位于非军事区以南200公里的一个城镇，仅仅是因为当地的气候更适合

of his aged parents from whom he, like a dutiful son,
can not bear to be separated.
You should never use the name of Hu Han
Min in your dispatches because the censor will turn
pale at the sight of these three words for they recall
the existence of an Opposition in China. In the view
of the censor, there is no Opposition in China. Should
Hu Han Min rejoin the Nanking Government, you will not
be permitted to report the fact immediately abroad for
it will be necessary to allow the censors a few days to
accustom themselves to the idea of not deleting the
name of Hu Han Min any more. And even then, he will
permit you only to speak of the arrival of the leader
in the capital and not of his rejoining, for this would
constitute an admission that at one time an influential
leader of the Kuomintang had thought that all was not
well. In the eyes of the censor, everything is perfect.
For him, the communists have already all been exterminated
even though, despite this, he leaves you the right to
announce every day the fresh defeats they are sustaining.
Once again, we would like to say that here
we are only referring to the misdeeds of the censors who
sin, not with the intention of doing harm to others, but
simply through ignorance and timidity.
Then there is also the reckless censor, as
ignorant as the first kind, but less scrupulous. He
thinks it will be sufficient to cut out phrases in a
haphazard way. He plays at censoring like a child
playing at being a soldier or a detective.
The "China Weekly" has reproduced a part
of the criticism which we had written recently about the
censorship from the point of view of International Law.
To-day, we are rather treating this matter from the
practical point of view. The "Review" has adopted the
role of champion of equality. "Since," says the Weekly,
"Europeans and Americans have to submit to censorship,
why should not the Japanese submit?" The paper then
demands that the Shanghai-Nagasaki telegraph should be
made to submit to censorship.
We have already expressed our views on
this subject. The Chinese censorship being absolutely
illegal, the Japanese are right not to submit. It is
up to the Europeans and the Americans to uphold respect
for their rights and to recall, among others, the terms
of the Washington Pact.
Nevertheless, if a Reuter's dispatch can
be believed, the Japanese authorities have consented to
discuss the question of the censorship of the Shanghai-
Nagasaki Cable with the Chinese Ministry of Foreign
Affairs.
After all, Sino-Japanese rapprochement
calls for some semblance of sacrifice on the part of
Japan. We say "semblance of sacrifice" advisedly,
because, whatever may be the official terms of the
future accord, everybody knows perfectly that the
censorship will not greatly trouble the Japanese
newspapermen. With them, it is a question of "face".
They will be assured that, if there are to be any censors,
they will be very obliging ones.
For our part, we do not ask for obliging
censors but censors who are at least intelligent and truly
competent. Those which are undertaking the censorship at
present understand nothing about their work. We demand
that a special school for censors be established and that
these censors be sent there.
G. M.

JAPANESE PRESS
TELEGRAMS
Chinese Government Claims
Right to Censorship

Nanking, May 26.
The right of the National Govern-
ment to censor press cables dispatch-
ed abroad through the Japanese cable
office in Shanghai is the subject of
negotiations being held between the
Chinese and Japanese authorities, it
is learnt in official circles.

The right to censor cables des-
patched by news agencies and press
correspondents in China, including
the Japanese, is claimed and exercis-
ed by the Chinese Government in ac-
cordance with Article 8 of the In-
ternational Telegraph Convention.

On the strength of this provision,
China has the right to detain or cen-
sor any cable messages which are
either factually incorrect or endan-
gering to the maintenance of peace
and order in China. Japanese cable
messages dispatched via the Shang-
hai-Nagasaki cable operated by the
Japanese in Shanghai must be sub-
ject to the same restrictions as is
maintained as are imposed on mes-
sages sent through the Eastern Ex-
tension (British), the Great Northern
(Danish), the Commercial Pacific
(American) cable routes and the
Chinese Government radio service.
—Kuo Min.

May 27, 1935.    3    Afternoon Translation.

Kiangnan Tsen Pao, a Japanese paper, published in the
Chinese language. (Nanking Telegram)

THE CENSORSHIP OF JAPANESE PRESS TELEGRAMS

The censorship of press telegrams by the
National Government has caused much misunderstanding to
the various foreign press. The censorship of press
telegrams by the Chinese Government is based on Article 26
of the International Telegraph and Postal Pact which stipu-
lates that the National Government reserves to itself the
right to detain, delete or amend incorrect telegrams or
any telegrams which are deemed to be dangerous to the
security or order of this country
Japanese press telegrams are sent through
the Shanghai-Nagasaki cable. However, at present negotiations
are in progress with the Japanese authorities and it is
probable that the Japanese press telegrams will be placed
on the same footing as other foreign telegrams.

GENERAL HUANG FU AND SINO-JAPANESE DISPUTES

General Huang Fu, Chairman of the Peiping
Political Reorganization Committee, arrived from Mokanshan
on May 23 and is now staying in French Concession, Shanghai.
It is reported that it is doubtful whether he will accept
the post of Minister of Interior, as he still intends to
refuse because the confused state of affairs in North
China has rendered fruitless his plans for a settlement of
Sino-Japanese disputes. It is understood that the present
attitude of General Huang Fu is due more or less to the
fact that his policy in dealing with Sino-Japanese questions
has not been entirely accepted by General Chiang Kai Shek,
Chairman of the Military Commission. This has caused great
uneasiness on the part of Wang Ching Wei, President of the
Executive Yuan, who immediately left Nanking for Shanghai
on the pretext of undergoing a physical examination, but in
reality to persuade General Huang Fu to cancel his resigna-
tion.

Eastern Daily News, a mosquito paper, published the following
article on May 24 written by a pedestrian.

MOTOR STREET SPRINKLERS OF THE S.M.C.

The principal object of the S.M.C. in
sending out motor sprinklers is to sprinkle water on streets
to remove the dust. But the drivers of these motor sprinklers
should not add to the annoyance of pedestrians while under-
taking this work. I have on several occasions noticed
drivers of the sprinklers purposely drenching pedestrians
thereby spoiling their garments. They regard this as a kind
of amusement.
The other day I saw two young girls walking
on the pavement opposite the Yellow Taxi Garage on Boundary
Road. When they heard the approach of a motor street
sprinkler coming up from behind, they endeavoured to avoid
being drenched, but the mischievous driver purposely drenched
them. The girls were annoyed, while the driver went off
joyfully.

1935年5月27日。    3    下午译文。

《江南申报》，一份以中文出版的日文报纸。（南京电）

日本新闻电报的审查

国民政府对新闻电报实施的审查，已引起各外国新闻界的诸多误解。中国政府对新闻电报的审查，依据的是《国际电报邮政公约》第26条，该条款规定国民政府保留扣留、删除或修改错误电报，或任何被认为危及本国安全或秩序的电报的权利。
日本新闻电报经由上海—长崎电缆发送。然而，目前正与日本当局进行谈判，日本新闻电报很可能将被置于与其他外国电报同等的地位。

黄郛将军与中日争端

北平政治整理委员会主席黄郛将军于5月23日从莫干山抵达，现寓居上海法租界。据报道，他是否接受内政部长一职尚存疑，因为他仍打算拒绝，原因是华北局势混乱，致使他解决中日争端的计划落空。据悉，黄郛将军目前的态度的产生，或多或少是因为军事委员会委员长蒋介石并未完全接受他处理中日问题的政策。这引起了行政院院长汪精卫的极大不安，汪精卫随即以体检为借口离开南京前往上海，实则是为了劝说黄郛将军撤销辞呈。

《东方日报》，一家小报，于5月24日刊登了一篇由一名路人撰写的文章。

工部局的机动街道洒水车

工部局派出机动洒水车的主要目的是向街道洒水以清除灰尘。但是，这些机动洒水车的司机在执行此项工作时，不应增加行人的烦恼。我曾多次注意到，洒水车司机故意淋湿行人，从而弄脏他们的衣物。他们将此视为一种娱乐。
前几天，我看见两名年轻女孩走在边界路（Boundary Road）黄色出租车车库对面的人行道上。当她们听到身后有一辆机动街道洒水车驶来时，便努力避免被淋湿，但那个恶作剧的司机故意将她们淋湿。女孩们很恼火，而司机则欢快地离开了。

May 26, 1935. Morning translation.

THE CENSORSHOP OF JAPANESE PRESS TELEGRAMS

The National Government has instituted a
censorship of Press telegrams. This action is based
or Article 26 of the International Telegraph and
Postal Pact which stipulates that the National
Government has the right to detain, delete or alter
incorrect telegrams or any telegrams which endanger
the security of the country.

In view of the fact that the Japanese are
transmitting Press telegrams by the Shanghai-Nagasaki
cable which is not supervised by the Chinese Authorities,
the National Government will open negotiations over the
matter with the Japanese Authorities.

日本新闻电报的审查

国民政府已实施新闻电报审查。此举依据的是《国际电报邮政公约》第26条，该条款规定国民政府有权扣留、删除或更改错误电报，或任何危及国家安全的电报。

鉴于日本人通过不受中国当局监管的上海—长崎电缆传输新闻电报，国民政府将就此事与日本当局展开谈判。

SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE
S. B. REGISTRY.
D.C. (CRIME) 2398
Date 2 / 5 / 35

May 2, 1935.
Afternoon Translation.

Journal de Shanghai : -

AN INEFFICIENT AND ILLEGAL CENSORSHIP

In the "China Weekly Review", a
Sino-American periodical published in Shanghai, of April 20
appears the following comment:-
"The inability of the Chinese Ministry
of Communications to exercise control over the Japanese
Telegraph Office which operates between Shanghai and
Nagasaki, is attracting the attention of diplomatic circles
in Shanghai, Nanking and Peiping. Such is a report
circulating this week in Shanghai. It is not known whether
protests have already been made but it is declared that the
American, British and Danish Ministers to China are studying
the question with the intention of pointing out to Nanking
this difference in treatment which is harmful to non-
Japanese interests in the matter of commercial censorship
and the censorship of news sent from Shanghai to foreign
countries".

In other words, the "China Weekly Review"
claims that the American, British and Danish Ministers to
China are complaining that the Chinese Government is not
imposing a censorship on Japanese telegrams, while a
rigorous censorship is being imposed on telegrams sent by
American, British, Danish and other people.
We do not believe that the writer
of the article in the "China Weekly Review" has correctly
expressed the feeling of the Ministers mentioned.
We can not believe that these honourable diplomats have
set themselves up as purveyors of Chinese censorship.
It is certain that they have no intention to stand in the
way so long as the countries which they represent are
honestly and loyally informed of the situation in the Far
East. We rather think that having ascertained that
telegrams dispatched by Japanese subjects are enjoying
absolute immunity in Shanghai, they are preparing to
take up the matter with the Chinese Government not with
the intention of demanding that a censorship be also
imposed on Japanese telegrams but that the absurd and
illegal censorship of American, British and Danish
telegrams be abolished.

It is probable that the eminent
personalities mentioned by the "China Weekly Review" are
not pleased with the establishment of a Chinese censorship
in the International Settlement. It is, in fact, certain
that the existence of this censorship is at least as much
contrary to the statutes of the International Settlement
as the inspection of factories by delegates of the Nanking
Government or of the Kuomintang. Every-body recognizes
that if a censorship has to be exercised on Press news
received or dispatched in the Settlement, it should perhaps
have been undertaken by the Police. Finally, so long as
extra-territoriality remains, the exercising of a censorship
over foreigners enjoying this right belongs to the Consuls
or other representatives of States upon whom these foreigners
depend.

In Shanghai Japan has refused to admit
any illegal Chinese censorship being imposed on her
telegraph services. It is hardly likely that the representatives
of other foreign States can be alarmed over this refusal;
on the contrary, there is reason to believe that they will
demand that the rights of their nationals be respected in
the same as those of Japan.

D.C.（刑事）2398
日期 1935年5月2日

1935年5月2日。
下午译文。

《上海日报》：-

一项低效且非法的审查

在4月20日出版的中美期刊《密勒氏评论报》（China Weekly Review）上，出现了如下评论：-
“中国交通部无法控制运营于上海和长崎之间的日本电报局，这一情况正引起上海、南京和北平外交界的关注。这是本周在上海流传的一则报道。目前尚不清楚是否已提出抗议，但据称，美国、英国和丹麦驻华公使正在研究这一问题，意图向南京指出这种待遇上的差异，这在商业审查以及从上海发往国外的新闻审查方面，损害了非日本利益。”

换言之，《密勒氏评论报》声称，美国、英国和丹麦驻华公使抱怨中国政府未对日本电报实施审查，而对美国、英国、丹麦及其他人士发送的电报却实施严格审查。
我们不相信《密勒氏评论报》文章的作者正确表达了上述公使的感受。
我们无法相信这些尊贵的外交官会将自己树立为中国审查制度的提供者。
可以肯定的是，只要他们所代表的国家能够诚实且忠实地获知远东局势，他们就无意阻挠。我们反而认为，在确认日本臣民发出的电报在上海享有绝对豁免权后，他们正准备就此问题与中国政府交涉，其目的并非要求也对日本电报实施审查，而是废除对美国、英国和丹麦电报那种荒谬且非法的审查。

《密勒氏评论报》提到的那些显要人物可能对在国际租界设立中国审查制度感到不满。事实上，这种审查制度的存在，至少与南京政府或国民党代表检查工厂一样，违背国际租界的章程。众所周知，如果必须对在租界内接收或发出的新闻进行审查，或许应由警方来执行。最后，只要治外法权依然存在，对享有此权利的外国人行使审查权，就属于这些外国人所依赖的领事或其他国家代表的职权范围。

在上海，日本拒绝承认对其电报服务施加任何非法的中国审查。其他外国国家的代表不太可能因这一拒绝而感到惊慌；相反，有理由相信，他们将要求尊重其国民的权利，使其与日本国民享有同等待遇。

SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE
S. R. REGISTRY.
D
Date / /

May 2, 1935. Afternoon Translation.

As regards the censorship itself, it has to be confessed that it has never been more absurd, more incompetent and more inefficient than it is to-day. It continues to conceal news which everybody knows and it prohibits the dispatch to foreign lands of information which, despite its impotent veto, is published by newspapers in Japan, Europe and America much earlier than the Chinese newspapers.

The day before yesterday, the Chinese Censorship did not want foreign countries to know the communist armies were only 30 kilometres from Yunnanfu. On the other hand, it allowed to be published a false report that the reds had made a half-turn and were returning in haste to Kweichow Province. Only, it seems to have overlooked the fact that there is no Chinese censorship at Hongkong or Dairen or Nagasaki or Tokyo.

Yesterday morning, while nearly all the newspapers of Shanghai were silent over events in Yunnan, all the papers in France and America received from Hongkong and Hanoi very accurate information to the effect that the communists were 25 kilometres from Yunnanfu, that they had captured Changpo and Yanglin and that most of the foreigners had been evacuated into Tonkin.

48 hours behind the newspapers of Indo-China and Europe, the censors yesterday morning decided to allow to pass a message from a Chinese source admitting the reds were 15 miles from Yunnanfu.

We have no intention whatever to dispute the right of the Chinese Government to exercise the strictest censorship over newspapers in China; we also recognize that, no matter how absurd the censors may be, they may act with as great severity as they wish outside the Settlements, even if they will allow to reach us only reports that are favourable to the cause which they believe they are serving so usefully.

But what is as intolerable as it is illegal is that items of news which they allow to circulate in China are not allowed to be telegraphed abroad by us; and what is also as inadmissible as it is grotesque is that they presume to compel us to think according to the Chinese way and to adopt the viewpoint of the official Chinese journalists and the often childish terms which they are obliged to use to designate such political personages as Pou Yi or such a region, as Manchuria. For the censors have as much fear of words as the hares of its shadow.

In any case, it is inadmissible that the question of the censorship of telegrams for abroad should be settled by an ordinary private agreement between the Chinese Minister of Communications and the Danish telegraph companies. Here is a singular idea of international law.

The censorship should not have been installed in the offices of the Northern Telegraph Co. and the Eastern Telegraph Co. without the formal consent of the foreign diplomatic authorities; besides, even if this consent had been given, the censorship should have been exercised over foreigners with the consent only of the responsible foreign censors.

上海公共租界工部局警务处
S. R. 登记处。
D
日期 / /

1935年5月2日。下午译文。

至于审查制度本身，必须承认，它从未像今天这样荒谬、无能和低效。它继续隐瞒众人皆知的新闻，并禁止向国外发送信息，尽管其否决权无力，这些信息在日本、欧洲和美国的报纸上刊登的时间远早于中国报纸。

前天，中国审查机构不希望外国知道共产党军队距离云南府仅30公里。另一方面，它允许发布一则虚假报道，称赤匪已掉头，正匆忙返回贵州省。只是，它似乎忽略了一个事实，即香港、大连、长崎或东京没有中国审查机构。

昨天上午，当上海几乎所有报纸对云南事件保持沉默时，法国和美国的所有报纸都从河内和西贡收到了非常准确的信息，称共产党人距离云南府25公里，他们已占领昌坡（Changpo）和杨林（Yanglin），且大多数外国人已撤离至东京湾（Tonkin）。

比印度支那和欧洲的报纸晚了48小时，审查员昨天上午决定放行一条来自中方来源的消息，承认赤匪距离云南府15英里。

我们绝无意质疑中国政府对中国境内报纸实施最严格审查的权利；我们也承认，无论审查员多么荒谬，他们在租界之外可以按照自己的意愿严厉行事，即使他们只允许向我们传递那些有利于他们认为自己在有效服务的事业的消息。

但是，既不可容忍又非法的是，他们允许在中国境内流传的新闻项目，却不允许我们通过电报发往国外；同样既不可接受又荒谬的是，他们妄图强迫我们按照中国人的方式思考，并采纳中国官方记者的观点，以及他们被迫用来称呼溥仪等政治人物或满洲等地区的往往幼稚的术语。因为审查员对文字的恐惧，就像兔子害怕自己的影子一样。

无论如何，不可接受的是，发往国外的电报审查问题应由中华民国交通部长与丹麦电报公司之间的一项普通私人协议来解决。这是对国际法的一种奇特理解。

未经外国外交当局的正式同意，审查机构本不应设在北方电报公司和东方电报公司的办公室内；此外，即使给予了这种同意，对外国人行使审查权也应仅在负责的外国审查员同意的情况下进行。

S. B. REGISTER
File No. D 2398
SHANGHAI MUNICIPAL POLICE.
S.1, Special Branch 1:35
REPORT
Date April 27, 1936.
Subject Japanese Telegraph Office.
Made by D.S.I. Duncan Forwarded by H. Grubbs C.O!

The Japanese Telegraph Office, No.25 Seward Road,
is an official government concern and therefore is not
subject to control by the Ministry of Communications of the
National Government as in the case of other telegraph
companies which are purely commercial concerns.
The employees of the Japanese Telegraph Office
are all officials of the Japanese Ministry of Communications
and, as such, are liable to be transferred to any telegraphic
office within the Japanese Empire.
Any foreigners may make use of this office
provided that all messages are handed to the receiving
office in the Japanese language, either characters or
romanisation.
The French Radio Station, 135 Route Prelupt, is
another case in point where the Chinese Authorities are
not in a position to exercise censorship as it is an
official organ of the French Council and therefore under
the control of the French Government. Although no
commercial news is broadcast over this Station, official
messages are exchanged between the local French Consular
Authorities and France or her colonies.

（印：OFFICE OF COMMISSIONER OF POLICE SHANGHAI）

位于西华德路25号的日本电报局是一家官方政府机构，因此不像其他纯属商业机构的电报公司那样受国民政府交通部的管辖。
日本电报局的雇员均为日本通信省官员，因此可能被调往日本帝国境内的任何电报局。
任何外国人均可使用该局，前提是所有消息必须以日语（汉字或罗马拼音形式）提交给收报处。
位于蒲石路135号的法国无线电台是另一个例子，中国当局无法在此行使审查权，因为它是法国公董局的官方机构，因此受法国政府控制。虽然该台不广播商业新闻，但当地法国领事当局与法国或其殖民地之间会交换官方消息。

APR. 27, 1935 THE CHINA WEEKLY REVIEW
LACK OF CENSORSHIP ON JAP CABLE
CAUSE OF DISTORTED NEWS
THE People's Tribune, edited by Tang Leang-li, which is popularly supposed to represent the political views of Wang Ching-wei, head of the National Executive Yuan at Nanking, published an article in its issue of April 16 complaining at the "nonsense and extravagant statements" which have been published abroad regarding the recent Sino-Japanese conversations pertaining to resumption of normal relations between the two countries. Readers of The Review who have followed reports which appeared in our issues of March 23 and April 20, dealing with the censorship situation at Shanghai are doubtlessly already familiar with the chief reason for the publication of so-called "distorted" reports regarding the Sino-Japanese conversations which have appeared in newspapers throughout the world. But to put it briefly, the chief reason for this situation has been due to Nanking's inability, or at least failure up to the present, to establish its censorship over news and commercial messages filed by Japanese correspondents and merchants, and transmitted to Japan over the Japanese cable between Shanghai and Nagasaki. The fact that the Chinese censorship authorities have not been able to establish their control over the Japanese cable, as they have over the cables and radio services used by Americans and Europeans, has had a disastrous effect on opinion abroad with respect to China's position in the recent Sino-Japanese negotiations. The reason for this deplorable situation is due to the fact that while news messages dispatched by American and European correspondents to newspapers abroad have been subjected to severe censorship, there has been no interference with messages filed by Japanese correspondents over the Japanese cable. As a result the Japanese have been able to place their own interpretation on recent developments in Nanking and these interpretations, in due course, have been telegraphed all over the world by newspaper correspondents stationed in Tokyo. Under ordinary conditions, political developments in China which are of international consequence, are cabled abroad by all correspondents, Americans, Europeans and Japanese. Each correspondent may place his own interpretation on the particular event, or he may interpret it in the light of his own country's interests in China, but when there is no restriction on cabled messages, newspaper readers abroad are able to compare reports and thus obtain a balanced view of what is going on. Ordinarily the American and European newspaper correspondent base their messages upon statements, official and unofficial, which appear in the local press, or they may telegraph interviews obtained from Chinese officials directly. Japanese newspapermen follow a similar course, although they are more inclined to shade their messages in accordance with the views of Japanese officialdom, particularly the military. Newspapers abroad, that is, in the United States, Great Britain and Continent, receive dispatches from all possible sources in the Far East, but chiefly from Nanking, Shanghai and Tokyo. In the event there is no censorship, or even in the case where a censorship is enforced impartially on newspapermen of all nationalities, the newspaper in Washington, New York, London, Paris, Berlin, Rome or Moscow is able to obtain a balanced viewpoint of developments. But in the event of the censorship being enforced on only one particular group, as has been the case here, the result naturally is disastrous because the newspaper editors and readers, in consequence, must base their opinions on one-sided reports. This is exactly what has been happening here with respect to the non-censorship of reports

1935年4月27日 《密勒氏评论报》
日本电报缺乏审查
导致新闻失实

由唐良礼（Tang Leang-li，音译）编辑、被普遍认为代表南京国民政府行政院长汪精卫政治观点的《人民论坛报》（The People's Tribune），在其4月16日刊出的一篇文章中，对国外就近期旨在恢复中日正常关系的中日会谈所发表的“胡言乱语和夸大其词”表示不满。阅读过本刊3月23日和4月20日有关上海新闻审查状况报道的读者，无疑已经熟悉世界各地报纸刊登所谓关于中日会谈“失实”报道的主要原因。简而言之，造成这种局面的主要原因在于，南京方面无力，或者至少截至目前未能，对日本记者和商人通过上海与长崎之间的日本海底电报线发往日本的新闻和商业电文实施审查。中国审查当局未能像对美国人和欧洲人使用的电缆及无线电服务那样，对日本电报线建立控制，这一事实对海外舆论 regarding 中国在近期中日谈判中的立场产生了灾难性影响。造成这种令人遗憾局面的原因在于，虽然美国和欧洲记者发往国外报纸的新闻电文受到严格审查，但日本记者通过日本电报线发送的电文却未受任何干扰。结果，日本人得以按照自己的意图解读南京近期的事态发展，而这些解读随后由驻东京的报社记者电传至世界各地。在通常情况下，具有国际影响的中国政治动态，会由所有记者——美国人、欧洲人和日本人——电传至国外。每位记者可能会根据特定事件发表自己的解读，或者根据其本国在华利益进行解读，但当电文不受限制时，海外报纸读者能够比较各方报道，从而获得对事态发展的平衡看法。通常，美国和欧洲报纸记者的报道基于当地报刊上出现的官方或非官方声明，或者直接电传从中国政府官员处获得的采访内容。日本记者也采取类似做法，尽管他们更倾向于根据日本官方、特别是军方的观点来修饰其报道。海外报纸，即在美国、英国和欧洲大陆的报纸，接收来自远东各方的电讯，但主要来自南京、上海和东京。如果不存在审查，或者即使对所有国籍的记者公平地实施审查，华盛顿、纽约、伦敦、巴黎、柏林、罗马或莫斯科的报纸都能够获得对事态发展的平衡观点。但如果审查仅针对某一特定群体实施，如此处的情形，结果自然是灾难性的，因为报纸编辑和读者因此必须依据片面报道形成观点。这正是此处因对经
